<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }
</style></head>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" title="In 3.1 Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agent configuration.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" title="In 3.1 Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Infrastructure and evaluation.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S3.SS2" title="In 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">3.2 </span>Main Results</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Frontier agents are still far from solving long-horizon professional
computer use.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Claude Opus 4.8 reaches higher accuracy while GPT-5.5 is more token-efficient.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Each additional point of accuracy costs disproportionately more
tokens.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">More turns do not buy completion; the turn-space frontier is set by
batching, not by taking more steps.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Extra inference buys partial credit, not completion, and the hard
“last mile” is the strict completion threshold.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Binary completion rate collapses as the task horizon grows.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7" title="In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier
models have opposite capability profiles.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S4" title="In OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4 </span>Analysis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS1" title="In 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.1 </span>Agent Behavior</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#S4.SS1.SSS1" title="In 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.1.1 </span>Solution Strategies</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsubsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1" title="In 4.1.1 Solution Strategies ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Across the 108 tasks, the behavior-analysis models reached only partial progress in most cases
rather than a complete solution.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2" title="In 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.1.2 </span>Action Patterns</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsubsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1" title="In 4.1.2 Action Patterns ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents spend most of their budget understanding the task.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2" title="In 4.1.2 Action Patterns ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Every model spends almost none of its budget on detecting and
fixing its own mistakes.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS2" title="In 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.2 </span>Agent Safety Analysis</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS3" title="In 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.3 </span>Human vs. Model Difficulty Gap</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS4" title="In 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.4 </span>Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents miss information from the instruction, the environment, or the user channel.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents fail on time-sensitive tasks when long observation-to-action gaps make their actions target stale interface states.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents struggle with interpreting and generating domain-specific artifacts.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents often fail to verify task-critical properties and correct errors they have already noticed before submission.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Agents forget information gathered early when task state is stored only in compressed reasoning or chain-of-thought context.</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6" title="In 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways.</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-6.0pt;"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/favicon.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:28/28;" width="28" height="28" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> XLANG Lab and Collaborators
</span><span id="id3" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Full contributor list and acknowledgments are provided in Appendix˜<a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Contributions and Acknowledgments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing computer-use benchmarks fail to capture the realism, complexity, and long-horizon demands of real-world computer use, limiting their ability to reveal the limitations of frontier agents.
We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, a benchmark of 108 long-horizon computer-use workflows across everyday and professional tasks, designed to capture complex and challenging real-world phenomena.
Each task represents a realistic end-to-end workflow that takes human users a median of about 1.6 hours to complete and requires an average of 318 tool calls with Claude Opus 4.7 using maximum thinking, compared with about  30 in <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span>.
<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> targets challenge phenomena that are common in real workflows yet underrepresented in prior benchmarks, spanning interaction-design challenges such as streaming interaction and dynamic environments, as well as agent-pattern challenges such as cross-source reasoning, implicit-state inference, and visual-spatial precision.
Tasks are grounded in authentic input artifacts and cross-referenced against realistic stateful user profile data, and include separate safety reports auditing safety-sensitive execution.
Under our primary binary-completion metric at 500 steps, Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and batched tool calls scores best but still completes only 20.6% of tasks at a 54.8% partial score; GPT-5.5 is far more token-efficient yet plateaus near 13%.
These results show that current agents are still far from professional-level computer use: rather than stumbling on basic GUI control or coding, they lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification, struggling most when a task hinges on hidden state they must recover.</p>
  
</div><span class="ltx_rule ltx_align_center ltx_align_bottom" style="width:0.0pt;height:6.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span>
<div id="id4" class="ltx_logical-block">
    
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="p1.1" class="ltx_inline-block fas fa-globe ltx_align_center" aria-hidden="true">
</span>
<p id="p1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Website:
<a href="https://osworld-v2.xlang.ai" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#1B4F9C;">osworld-v2.xlang.ai</a></p>
</div>
  
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/main_figure_v.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/234;" width="452" height="234" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Left: A representative <span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> workflow: submitting an ExpenseFlow
reimbursement claim.
The agent must follow a tutorial PDF, operate a legacy reimbursement portal,
extract the correct amount from noisy receipt artifacts, trace order evidence
across GMail and ChaseBank, react to a new email that changes the task
state, recover hidden employee information from a prior report, gather
supporting documents across applications, identify an inconsistency that
requires user clarification, and complete final review and submission.
Right: A sweep of model performance under
different reasoning-effort levels, plotted against output tokens per task. Even with more reasoning
effort, model scores on <span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> remain far below their <span id="S0.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span> performance.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">People use computers for a wide range of everyday and professional work, from
web browsing and document editing to data analysis and software development.
Powered by recent vision-language models, computer-use agents can now attempt
such work directly from natural-language instructions: commercial systems such
as Claude Cowork <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026a</a>]</cite> and OpenAI Codex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025b</a>]</cite>,
together with open-source agents such as OpenClaw <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenClaw Contributors, 2026</a>]</cite>, browse
the web, manage files, write and run code, and operate desktop applications on a
user’s behalf.
They promise to make computers more accessible and productive, yet evaluation has
not kept pace with their deployment, and it remains unclear how much of this
real-world work they can actually complete.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing benchmarks fall short of capturing real-world computer-use performance.
While Claude Opus 4.8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026b</a>]</cite> reaches 83.5% on OSWorld-Verified <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>]</cite>, suggesting desktop computer use is largely solved, the tasks behind this number are short and narrow, rarely spanning more than one or two applications, and reward completing self-contained actions rather than sustaining long, connected workflows.
High accuracy on such benchmarks therefore overstates real progress and obscures how rarely agents complete the end-to-end work that real deployment demands.
Yet no existing benchmark is simultaneously long-horizon, grounded in a realistic operating environment, and rich in the complex phenomena that real workflows entail.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To bridge this gap, we introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, a benchmark
of 108 long-horizon, real-world computer-use tasks.
The median task takes a skilled human about 1.6 hours of active operation,
roughly <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="48\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">48\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer than OSWorld 1.0, and leading agents average more than
300 steps per task, against about 30 in OSWorld 1.0.
Three principles shape the benchmark.
First, <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">authentic workflows</em>: tasks come from real professional scenarios
surfaced through expert interviews and trained-annotator research, with input
artifacts collected or adapted from real materials rather than synthesized.
Second, <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">long-horizon structure</em>: each task’s difficulty comes from a
workflow that decomposes into interdependent steps across multiple applications,
not from repetition or the concatenation of unrelated subtasks.
Third, <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diverse challenge phenomena</em>: every task is annotated with ten
phenomena, such as cross-source reasoning, implicit-state inference, conflict
disambiguation, and dynamic environments, that each probe a distinct capability
and jointly stress the structural demands of real work.
To realize them, <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> self-hosts 31 task-facing web services such as email,
banking, and team chat with controlled, scoreable states, seeds each task from a
coherent stateful user profile, injects mid-task messages so the environment
changes under the agent, and exposes a simulated user with bounded knowledge.
We score the final state against fine-grained checkpoints (averaging 27.25 per
task), favoring functional checks over bounded model-based judgment, and audit
every task through generated unit tests, human re-solving, and frontier-agent
rollouts against both reward hacking and false negatives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We run cost-aware evaluations of current agents, including Claude Opus 4.8 and 4.7, GPT-5.5, and leading open-source models, under 150-, 300-, and 500-step budgets.
Even the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and
batched tool calls, completes only 20.6% of tasks under strict binary
completion while reaching 54.8% partial score, and GPT-5.5, the most
token-efficient agent, plateaus near 13% at under a fifth of Opus’s token
budget, so higher completion comes only at a steeply rising token cost.
Completion is also fragile to horizon: it collapses toward zero on the longest
workflows even as partial scores stay high, and tasks humans find easy often
remain hard for agents, so progress transfers only partially from horizon-based
scaling laws.
These failures are not about basic GUI control or coding.
Across our analysis, agents execute local actions well but cannot hold a
task-level model together over a long horizon: they drop stated constraints, miss
information that arrives mid-task, guess instead of asking the user, and skip the
verification that completion depends on, and they spend almost none of their
budget (under 7%) on detecting and repairing their own errors.
These weaknesses concentrate on phenomena that demand recovering and maintaining
hidden state, namely implicit-state inference, multi-item state tracking,
conflict disambiguation, and dynamic environments.
Progress here therefore depends less on longer budgets or larger models than on
agents that can act on streaming, continuously changing interfaces, keep a
task-level model in memory across long horizons, and catch and repair their own
mistakes before they propagate.
We release the environment, the 108 tasks, the self-hosted websites, and agent
rollout trajectories to support future research in this direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> Benchmark</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> builds on the OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>]</cite> evaluation platform and
extends it with improvements in task scope, environment design, task complexity,
and evaluation methodology.
Table <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix B OSWorld 1.0 vs. OSWorld 2.0: Key Improvements ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (Appendix) summarizes the key advances.
The following subsections describe how tasks are designed and constructed
(§<a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>) and then summarize the resulting task set
(§<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Task Design and Construction</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each task in <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> is defined as a self-contained end-to-end workflow
that an agent must complete given a high-level user goal, realistic artifacts,
a stateful computer environment, and a scoreable final state.
A retained task must satisfy two design criteria.
First, it must be long-horizon: its difficulty should come from interdependent
workflow structure rather than repetition or concatenated subtasks.
This structure may span several applications through real information
dependencies, or stay within one application while requiring the agent to plan,
execute, and verify a complete result.
Second, it must be realistic: task-relevant information is grounded in authentic
artifacts and workspace state, and is often distributed across files,
applications, web services, and prior records rather than written entirely into
the prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Constructing these tasks raised two linked challenges.
First, we needed to find workflows with enough real-world complexity.
Second, we needed to turn those workflows into clear benchmark tasks with
reproducible environments and reliable evaluation.
Long workflows are hard to audit: small errors can accumulate over many steps,
and strong agents can sometimes exploit vague scoring criteria, earning credit
without completing the intended workflow.
We therefore organize construction as a pipeline: collect candidate workflows
(§<a href="#S2.SS1.SSS1" title="2.1.1 Task Collection ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.1</span></a>), instantiate them as reproducible computer
environments (§<a href="#S2.SS1.SSS2" title="2.1.2 Environment Setup ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.2</span></a>), define final-state evaluation
(§<a href="#S2.SS1.SSS3" title="2.1.3 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.3</span></a>), and audit the resulting tasks through
multi-layer quality assurance (§<a href="#S2.SS1.SSS4" title="2.1.4 Annotation and Quality Assurance ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.1 </span>Task Collection</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Production-grade workflows are rarely shared publicly because they often involve
sensitive data, proprietary toolchains, or domain-specific conventions.
Public materials therefore skew toward introductory tutorials or isolated pain
points rather than complete cross-tool pipelines.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Other strategies. ‣ 2.1.1 Task Collection ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we combine four
collection strategies in this proposal stage, with team brainstorming and
expert-style annotation as the primary source and the other channels as
supporting sources.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Team brainstorming and expert-style annotation.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The bulk of <span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> tasks were produced by a small group of internally
trained annotators who worked end-to-end on the tasks they proposed,
covering task design, input artifact construction, environment setup, and
evaluation function implementation.
Annotators first learned the target domain by watching tutorials on
YouTube, reading official documentation, and directly experimenting with the
software, which equipped them to reason about professional tools and workflows, or enterprise systems in sufficient depth.
They then drafted candidate tasks grounded in workflows surfaced from
Reddit discussions, online tutorials, and their own day-to-day work
experience, with each draft specifying the instructions, required input
artifacts, and expected final state.
Every candidate was finally peer cross-checked by a second annotator, who
reviewed it for feasibility, redundancy with existing tasks, and ambiguity
in the evaluation criteria; rejected drafts were either revised or
discarded, and surviving candidates entered the implementation and
audit stages described later.
This channel ultimately produced approximately <span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">90%</span> of the final tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Other strategies.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We supplemented the brainstorming pipeline with three additional channels,
each contributing only a small fraction of the final benchmark.
Semi-structured <span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">interviews</span> with practitioners, anchored on public
job descriptions and LLM-generated seed operations, produced
high-quality candidates but were expensive to scale.
<span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Questionnaires</span> asking respondents to describe a task, provide
input files, and specify the expected deliverable were fast to distribute
but yielded few retained tasks, since respondents struggled to calibrate
complexity and rarely engaged in the follow-up needed to recover missing
context.
<span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthetic task proposals</span> generated by an LLM expanded the
candidate pool rapidly but showed three recurring problems: unrealistic
input artifacts, shallow workflows that compose unrelated operations, and
reward-hacking risks arising from designs that fail to anticipate
alternative valid solutions. We therefore treat synthetic generation as an
idea-generation aid rather than a replacement for human task design.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/os2_tasks_final1_pipeline.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/206;" width="476" height="206" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Task construction pipeline for <span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
Task ideas are collected from team brainstorming, interviews, questionnaires,
and synthetic proposals, then filtered by complexity, diversity, and
feasibility before being converted into executable task specifications.
Construction configures self-hosted web services, applications, initial and
final workspace states, simulated user channels, and dynamic-update hooks
before the resulting tasks undergo iterative quality assurance, including unit-test
generation, human cross-checking, trajectory rollouts, and targeted reviews
for feasibility, partial rewards, and reward-hacking risks.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.2 </span>Environment Setup</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After a candidate workflow passes the proposal filter, annotators convert it
into a reproducible computer environment. As in <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span>, agents operate in a
real desktop environment, but <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> adds task-facing services, richer
workspace state, simulated user interaction, and dynamic updates so that the
environment itself carries task-relevant information.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Web services and applications.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Realistic computer-use work passes through both local applications and
stateful web services. <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> therefore recreates task-facing web services such as
email inboxes, banking portals, team chat, and business portals in self-hosted
form with controlled initial and scoreable final states, preserving the
realism of web-based work while avoiding the layout drift, anti-bot blocks,
and unreproducible histories of live third-party sites.
Beyond the common desktop applications of <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span> (LibreOffice, GIMP, VLC,
Thunderbird, VS Code, Chrome), <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> also extends to social platforms
(Slack, LinkedIn), creative software (Shotcut, REAPER, MuseScore), office
collaboration tools (WPS, GitLab, Overleaf), scientific and academic tools
(LabPlot, Zotero, AWS), and professional services (insurance claim, visa
application, and conference management portals).
These applications and services serve as workflow surfaces rather than
isolated UI demos: agents must coordinate across the software boundaries, file
formats, and handoffs real users encounter.
The full website list and deployment details appear in
§<a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Self-hosted Websites ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> and
Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Website Framework ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>; desktop coverage is summarized in
Appendices <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Desktop Applications ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a> and <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Application Coverage Analysis ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Initial environment states.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each task begins from a task-specific workspace rather than a blank desktop.
The setup can include local files, open documents or browser tabs, self-hosted
website states, account records, prior messages, downloaded artifacts, and
reference material.
Annotators keep these materials aligned around a coherent user profile and
workflow state, so identifiers, dates, amounts, prior submissions, and message
histories agree across sources.
Artifacts are collected from or adapted from realistic materials where possible;
synthetic records are used only when needed for privacy, release, or
controllability, and are made consistent with the task constraints and scoreable
final state.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Simulated user.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some realistic tasks contain missing evidence, ambiguous constraints, or
conflicting records that cannot be resolved from the environment alone.
For these cases, the task setup includes a simulated user with bounded
task-specific knowledge.
When an agent asks for clarification through the user channel, the simulator
returns an answer grounded only in that configured knowledge, allowing tasks to
evaluate whether agents know when to pause, ask, and incorporate the response
without relying on an interactive human evaluator.
We validate this simulated user component separately in
Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dynamic environment.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Controlled services also let a task change while the agent is working.
<span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> can inject task-relevant emails or TeamChat messages during
execution, testing whether agents continue monitoring relevant channels,
notice new constraints, and revise earlier decisions instead of treating the
first observed state as final.
This differs from streaming interaction: dynamic environment tasks change the
semantic task state, whereas streaming interaction changes the visual state
between observation and action.
Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS2" title="H.2.2 Task 035: Dynamic Environment ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.2</span></a> illustrate these dynamically updated
workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.3 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h4>

<section id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fine-grained partial reward.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span> uses binary pass/fail scoring, which works for short tasks but is too coarse for the long-horizon workflows in <span id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
It assigns the same score to an agent that makes no meaningful progress and one that completes most subtasks but misses a final verification step.
We therefore use fine-grained partial rewards with task-specific checkpoints, averaging 27.25 checkpoints per task.
To support different valid solution paths, we score the final environment state against all checkpoints rather than a fixed checkpoint order.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Functional and model-based evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We prioritize functional evaluation whenever possible, using checks over concrete environment states and output artifacts.
But some tasks require more open-ended judgments, such as whether an edited image meets visual requirements or whether an email is contextually appropriate.
For these cases, we use model-based evaluation as a limited complement, with objective binary checklists instead of open-ended grading.
Each judge prompt is validated on labeled correct and confusable incorrect states across supported judge models, and is accepted only when it is consistently accurate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, model-based evaluation contributes 11.53% of the total score, and no task relies on it for more than 50%.
Detailed statistics are reported in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.4 </span>Annotation and Quality Assurance</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Once a candidate becomes an executable task specification, it enters the
three-stage quality-assurance stack shown on the right of
Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Other strategies. ‣ 2.1.1 Task Collection ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
A coding agent first generates an initial battery of unit tests that
implement the scoring rubric and exercise the expected solution paths.
Two independent human annotators then complete the task end-to-end and
cross-check whether the instruction is solvable from the provided
environment, whether the rubric captures the intended outcome, and whether
the scoring checkpoints cover the main workflow with balanced weights. Finally, the task is exercised by multiple frontier agents whose rollout
trajectories surface remaining gaps in the rubric and reveal solution
patterns that the original annotator may not have anticipated.
Disagreements at any stage trigger task or rubric revision, and tasks that
remain infeasible or ambiguous are removed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these stages check both task validity and evaluation reliability.
For task validity, we verify that each task is solvable from the instruction
and environment as written, and that the partial-reward checkpoints correspond
to meaningful progress rather than shallow intermediate states.
For evaluation reliability, we audit two opposite scoring risks.
First, reward-hacking audits look for ways an agent could earn credit without
satisfying the user’s request, such as by exploiting files, APIs, browser
storage, or project metadata. These loopholes are surfaced through manual
review, adversarial tests generated by coding agents, and rollout inspection.
For example, if a task asks for the shortest walking route but the evaluator
only checks waypoints, an agent could earn credit for a driving route.
Second, false-negative audits check whether correct or acceptable solutions are
under-scored, for example because rigid state checks or model judges penalize
harmless formatting differences. When the valid output space is bounded, we
mitigate these cases with fuzzy functional checks or constrained model-based
evaluation; otherwise, we tighten the instruction or remove the task.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F4.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_bottom" style="width:186.3pt;"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure3.png" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:257/179;" width="257" height="179" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Human operation-time comparison between OSWorld 1.0 and
<span id="S2.F4.fig1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>. <span id="S2.F4.fig1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> has a median human operation time of approximately
1.6 hours, about 48 times longer than the roughly two-minute median in
OSWorld 1.0.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F4.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_bottom" style="width:144.9pt;"><img src="2606.29537v2/task_domain_dist.png" id="S2.F4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:200/200;" width="200" height="200" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Task domain distribution across seven professional domains
(inner ring) and 21 subcategories (outer ring).
Segment area is proportional to task count out of 108 tasks.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Task Overview</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> comprises 108 tasks across 31 self-hosted websites and a broad range
of desktop applications.
These tasks are designed to measure complete computer-use workflows rather than
isolated interface operations.
They require agents to work over long horizons, move across applications and
services, recover task-relevant state from realistic artifacts, and keep that
state consistent until the final submission or deliverable.
The benchmark also targets challenge phenomena that commonly appear in real
workflows but are weakly covered by prior benchmarks, including cross-source
reasoning, implicit-state inference, dynamic environments, streaming
interaction, proactive user interaction, tutorial following, and multimodal or
visual-spatial work.
As a result, the task set is broad not only in domain coverage, but also in the
types of reasoning, perception, interaction, and verification that agents must
perform.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1 </span>Task Statistics</h4>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task horizon.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> targets sustained workflows rather than short, isolated desktop
operations.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.1.4 Annotation and Quality Assurance ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the median human
operation time is approximately 1.6 hours, about <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="48\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>48</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">48\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer than the
roughly two-minute median in <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span>; 69.6% of tasks are estimated to take
a skilled human user more than one hour.
Agent trajectories show the same scale shift: <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span> averages roughly
30 steps, while <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> requires more than 250 steps per task under our
strongest evaluation setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The horizon is also cross-application.
With rollout usage included, each <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> task involves 2.44 apps or services
on average, compared with 1.35 in <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span>.
Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Task horizon. ‣ 2.2.1 Task Statistics ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports both required apps and rollout-observed apps.
We count each self-hosted website as an independent service, since these sites
replace real platforms such as email, banking, team chat, and application
portals; incidental open-web browsing is grouped under Chrome.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Percentage of tasks by number of apps and services.</figcaption>
<div id="S2.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:172.5pt;height:30pt;vertical-align:-13.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-56.2pt,9.8pt) scale(0.605627875202395,0.605627875202395) ;">
<table id="S2.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S2.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.6pt 3.2pt;"></td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.6pt 3.2pt;" colspan="6">Number of apps and services per task</td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td" style="padding:0.6pt 3.2pt;"></td>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By instruction and setup alone, 64.8% of tasks require two or more apps or
services; with rollout usage included, the share rises to 75.9%.
Single-app tasks are still substantial: they require deep use of specialized
creative, engineering, and scientific tools, or focused operation of a single
web service.
Appendix <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Application Coverage Analysis ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> reports the full app and website ranking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Professional-domain distribution.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2.1.4 Annotation and Quality Assurance ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the distribution of tasks across seven
professional domains and their 21 subcategories.
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Research &amp; Education</em> and <em id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Creative Production</em> together account
for over 40% of the benchmark.
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Engineering &amp; Computing</em> adds specialist technical workflows.
The remaining domains cover personal services, business and finance, and
administrative or compliance work.
The 21 subcategories keep the benchmark broad within each domain and reduce
the chance that success comes from a narrow domain shortcut.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/osworld_economic_coverage.svg" id="S2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/167;" width="381" height="167"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Economic coverage of <span id="S2.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> tasks. Left chart illustrates the economic representation by occupation-family category. The right table details each category’s absolute monetary contribution to the total GDP proxy.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Economic value.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Professional-domain distribution. ‣ 2.2.1 Task Statistics ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes a task-to-economic-value
mapping based on occupation families and SOC major groups.
We use a wage-bill-based GDP proxy to estimate the economic coverage of the
task set.
The largest mapped shares are document preparation (23.8%), software and
databases (17.8%), and finance and operations analysis (16.3%).
The remaining tasks cover a long tail of other professional activities.
Appendix <a href="#A7.SS1" title="G.1 Task-to-Economic-Value Mapping ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.1</span></a> gives the mapping rules and confidence-label procedure.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2 </span>Challenge Phenomena</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> tasks are annotated with non-exclusive tags for <em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">challenge
phenomena</em>: recurring bottlenecks that appear across realistic computer-use
workflows.
The ten phenomena cover all 108 tasks; a task may carry multiple tags, so
percentages in Table <a href="#S2.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 2.2.2 Challenge Phenomena ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> sum to more than 100%.
We use these tags for the exposure-attribution analysis in
Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7" title="Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier models have opposite capability profiles. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, and provide full definitions in
Appendix <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Challenge Phenomena Descriptions ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For instance, the reimbursement workflow in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, expanded in
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS1" title="H.1.1 Task 008: Expense Reimbursement ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.1</span></a>, illustrates four of
the phenomena in one task.
The task starts with an ExpenseFlow reimbursement guideline already open; the
agent must read the policy sections for account codes and upload requirements
before filling the legacy portal, which tests <em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Tutorial Following</em>.
The evidence is then split across GMail receipts and e-tickets, ChaseBank
travel charges, and a previous ExpenseFlow report containing
personal identifiers.
Matching these sources to the final claim tests <em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Cross-source Reasoning</em>.
The workflow is also dynamic: a new email can arrive while the agent is already
working, forcing it to revise the reimbursement plan and re-check earlier
decisions.
This captures <em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dynamic Environment</em>.
Finally, if the supporting evidence is incomplete or inconsistent, the agent
should ask the user before submitting the claim, which captures
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Proactive Interaction</em>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T2" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:36%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Challenge phenomena in <span id="S2.T2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.</figcaption>

<span id="S2.T2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S2.T2.4.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.T2.4.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phenomenon</span></span>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The other phenomena cover complementary bottlenecks.
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Streaming Interaction</em> captures continuously changing UI state, as in the
moving-popup booking task (Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS1" title="H.2.1 Task 052: Streaming Interaction ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.1</span></a>).
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Multimodal Editing</em> covers substantive image, video, audio, or 3D editing
(Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS4" title="H.2.4 Task 053: Multimodal Editing ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.4</span></a>).
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Visual-spatial Precision</em> appears in geometry- and layout-sensitive work,
such as FreeCAD reconstruction (Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS2" title="H.1.2 Task 103: FreeCAD Reconstruction ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.2</span></a>).
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Implicit-state Inference</em> covers hidden or unstated task state, such as
recovering employee information from a prior report in the reimbursement task.
<em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Multi-item State Tracking</em> and <em id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Conflict Disambiguation</em> cover
large structured item sets and stale or contradictory updates, as in the
purchase-order workflow and exposure examples
(Appendices <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS2" title="H.2.2 Task 035: Dynamic Environment ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.2</span></a>
and <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Challenge Exposure Attribution Details ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.3 </span>Comparison with Other Computer-Use Benchmarks</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The closest recent points of comparison for <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> are
MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>]</cite> and
Agents’ Last Exam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2026</a>]</cite>.
Earlier benchmarks such as <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 1.0</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>]</cite> and
WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>]</cite> provide real interactive environments, but
their tasks are mostly short and narrow.
<span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> shifts the unit of evaluation to complete long-horizon workflows.
Agents must carry information across applications, realistic artifacts, prior
records, and changing environment state until the final deliverable is complete.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MyPCBench centers evaluation on a coherent personalized desktop state, whereas
<span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> places greater stress on much longer workflow execution.
In MyPCBench, Claude Sonnet 4.6 averages 45.8 steps per task, while in
<span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> the stronger Claude Opus 4.7 still averages 318.4 steps per task.
This gap shows that the longer horizon in <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> is not due to weaker agents
spending more steps, but to workflows that require substantially more sustained
execution.
In <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, difficulty comes from end-to-end professional workflows that
combine long execution horizons, cross-application dependencies, specialized
desktop software, realistic input artifacts, and dense final-state evaluation.
This design makes the benchmark harder to solve by short lookup,
single-application action, or shallow personal-state retrieval alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Agents’ Last Exam is another close comparison, targeting professional and
economically valuable work.
ALE treats GUI interaction as part of a broader generalist-agent toolset,
alongside shell commands, file operations, code execution, web access, and API
calls, and only 34% of public task instances designate graphical software as
the primary tool.
By contrast, <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> makes GUI-based operation itself the central object of
evaluation.
Beyond this difference in tool focus, <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> also exposes agents to a wider
set of challenge phenomena that they must handle during execution.
Agents must preserve state across desktop applications, web services, files, messages, and prior records over hundreds of steps, while handling
streaming interaction, dynamic environments, proactive interaction, tutorial following, multimodal editing, visual-spatial precision, and multi-application state tracking.
This makes <span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> a harder and more diagnostic benchmark for agents that must operate real computers over long, stateful workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Setup</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate seven computer-use model families: Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7,
Claude Sonnet 4.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026c</a>]</cite>, GPT-5.5, Qwen 3.7-Plus,
MiniMax M3, and Kimi 2.6.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agent configuration.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All models use screenshot observations, and the step budget is 500. Claude models
act through the native
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude_computer_use</span> tool, while the remaining models emit
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pyautogui</span> code actions. Generation is capped at 16K output tokens, or
8K for MiniMax M3. A 3 s pause is inserted after each action. We test two
tool-use settings: <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">batched</em> (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">batch</span>; multiple tool calls per
step) and <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single</em> (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">std</span>; one call per step). GPT-5.5 always
batches its tool calls, whereas Claude models batch only when the batch tool is
explicitly enabled, so batched results cover GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We vary reasoning effort separately. Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> runs each model
at its highest thinking level (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">max</span> for the Claude models and
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">xhigh</span> for GPT-5.5), with Kimi 2.6 and MiniMax M3 simply thinking-on and
Qwen 3.7-Plus thinking-off, whereas the right panel of Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> sweeps
several thinking levels per model, one tested setting per point: <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">low</span>,
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">medium</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">high</span>, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">xhigh</span> for GPT-5.5, and those four
plus <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">max</span> for the Claude Opus models, with Sonnet 4.6 evaluated at
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">medium</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">max</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Infrastructure and evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Runs execute headlessly on AWS CPU instances in <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">us-east-1</span>, defaulting
to <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">t3.2xlarge</span> and using larger types when needed. Multiple environments
run in parallel. All web traffic is routed through a residential proxy.
Model-based evaluation and the human-in-the-loop user simulator both use Claude
Sonnet 4.6 (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>). All runs use release
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v2026.06.24</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">

<td id="S3.T3.4.8.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">326.7</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T3.4.9" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T3.4.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Kimi 2.6</th>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">4.6</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">22.1</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><math id="S3.T3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>$6.6</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">179.3</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">63.0K</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.9.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">179.3</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T3.4.10" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T3.4.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Qwen 3.7-Plus</th>
