<td id="S3.T3.4.10.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">28.9K</td>
<td id="S3.T3.4.10.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">173.5</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Frontier agents are still far from solving long-horizon professional
computer use.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and the right panel of Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> together
show how far current agents remain from solving <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
The best 500-step configuration in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, Claude Opus 4.8
with max thinking and the batched tool, reaches only 20.6% binary completion
and 54.8% partial score, while GPT-5.5 reaches 13.0% and Claude Opus 4.7
reaches 18.2%.
Plotting these runs against output tokens in the right panel of
Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> makes the gap concrete, since the same
frontier agents are saturated at 79–83% binary accuracy on OSWorld 1.0 but
sit an order of magnitude lower on <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
Current agents therefore make substantial partial progress, but under strict
completion criteria they leave most professional workflows unsolved.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Claude Opus 4.8 reaches higher accuracy while GPT-5.5 is more token-efficient.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Read as a cost-controlled comparison <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2024b</a>]</cite>, the
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> portion of the right panel of Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> splits capability from
efficiency across the two model families.
GPT-5.5 is the most token-efficient agent by a wide margin, reaching <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>14%
binary reward at only <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>37K output tokens per task while every Claude curve
is still in its lower-left region.
But GPT-5.5 plateaus there, with its 150-, 300-, and 500-step points all
converging near <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>14%, so the higher scores belong only to Claude.
Claude Opus 4.7 reaches 18.2% at around 150K tokens, while Claude Opus 4.8
reaches the best result on the benchmark, 20.5%, at around 225K.
This matches the broader finding that the highest-scoring agent is rarely the
most efficient one <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2025</a>]</cite>, so a small token budget favors GPT-5.5
while maximizing task completion regardless of cost calls for Claude Opus.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Each additional point of accuracy costs disproportionately more
tokens.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The frontier also steepens sharply toward the top, so the token cost of one more
point of binary reward rises by roughly an order of magnitude as agents approach
the ceiling.
Reaching the first <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>14% costs only <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>37K tokens with GPT-5.5, which is
a few thousand tokens per point, while pushing to 18.2% then takes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>150K
tokens with Claude Opus 4.7 and reaching 20.5% takes <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>225K with Claude
Opus 4.8, or roughly 25 to 30K extra tokens for each additional point.
The two Opus models show the same effect within one family, since Opus 4.8
spends about half again as many tokens as Opus 4.7 (around 225K versus 150K) for
only about two more points.
The remaining gap to full completion is therefore gated by a steeply rising
token cost rather than a fixed one, so closing it will demand disproportionately
more inference rather than marginally more.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/osworld2_turns_binary_chart.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:231/171;" width="231" height="171"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/osworld2_output_tokens_partial_chart.svg" id="S3.F6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:231/171;" width="231" height="171"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Two complementary views of the cost–performance frontier on
<span id="S3.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, each obtained from the binary-reward-versus-output-token panel of
Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> by swapping a single axis.
<span id="S3.F6.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> binary completion against average turns per task, swapping the
cost axis from tokens to turns.
<span id="S3.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> partial reward against average output tokens per task, swapping
the performance axis from strict completion to partial credit.
Each connected series sweeps one agent’s thinking or step-budget settings.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">More turns do not buy completion; the turn-space frontier is set by
batching, not by taking more steps.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The left panel of Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Each additional point of accuracy costs disproportionately more tokens. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> swaps the output-token axis
of Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for average turns per task, the number of times an
agent observes and acts against the environment.
Turns are the cost that matters for interactive deployment, since each one adds
latency and gives the interface another chance to shift underneath the agent.
The ranking inverts.
Claude Opus 4.8 is the most token-expensive agent on the benchmark yet one of the
cheapest in turns, reaching its benchmark-best 20.6% in only <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>103 turns
because batched calls let it act several times per turn.
Claude Opus 4.7 needs <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>190 turns for 18.2%, while the single-action
Sonnet 4.6 and MiniMax M3 sit far to the right at 250 to 325 turns for under 10%.
Cutting the number of environment turns an agent needs therefore matters as much
as cutting its token bill.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extra inference buys partial credit, not completion, and the hard
“last mile” is the strict completion threshold.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The right panel keeps the token axis but swaps binary completion for partial
reward, and the frontier flattens.
Every strong agent jumps into a tight band between 41% and 54%, far above the
8 to 20% spread in binary completion.
GPT-5.5 reaches <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>49.5% at only <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>37K tokens, essentially tying Claude
Opus 4.7, which needs <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>150K tokens for 48.9%, and coming within five points
of Opus 4.8’s best of 54.2% at <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>225K.
The same six-fold increase in tokens adds only <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>5 partial points here, yet
still separates 13% from 20% in the binary view of Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Scaling inference thus mostly converts into partial progress that all strong
agents reach cheaply, and Claude Opus’s real edge over GPT-5.5 is converting that
progress into finished tasks rather than making more of it.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Binary completion rate collapses as the task horizon grows.</h5>

<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/task_length_binary.svg" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/159;" width="238" height="159"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Binary completion accuracy by human-annotated expected task time.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Binary completion rate collapses as the task horizon grows. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> quantifies the central challenge of
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, since agent performance falls sharply as task length increases.
Among the models shown, GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 achieve 20–24% binary
completion accuracy on shorter tasks (under 45 minutes), but these success rates
decline rapidly as workflows extend, and by the 137–163 minute bin no model
exceeds 10% accuracy.
On the most extreme tasks (exceeding 163 minutes), binary completion falls to
zero for every model retained in the plot (see
Appendix <a href="#A7.SS2" title="G.2 Task-Length Binning and Binary Completion Statistics ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.2</span></a> for the time-binning methodology and
raw accuracy table).
Despite small fluctuations, the aggregate trend shows that task horizon remains a
hard limit for current agents.
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> workflows require sustained cross-application coordination and
information tracking, so longer horizons compound execution load and
state-management errors.
Current architectures can execute isolated short-horizon subtasks, but they do
not yet handle the structural depth required for end-to-end professional
workflows.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T4" class="ltx_table">

</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier
models have opposite capability profiles.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the ten challenge phenomena defined in
Section <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS2" title="2.2.2 Challenge Phenomena ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2.2</span></a>.
Because tags are non-exclusive, the same task can contribute to multiple
phenomena, and a raw phenomenon score alone does not establish that the
corresponding phenomenon caused an agent’s failure.
For example, a trajectory may fail before reaching the tutorial-dependent step,
or it may obtain apparent credit by directly manipulating hidden states rather
than solving the intended interaction problem.
We therefore use trajectory-level exposure attribution as the main diagnostic
view, labeling each trajectory as Handled, Blocked, or Untested
(Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Binary completion rate collapses as the task horizon grows. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), and report raw phenomenon scores
separately in Appendix <a href="#A7.SS4" title="G.4 Raw Challenge-Phenomenon Scores ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.4</span></a>.
For main Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier models have opposite capability profiles. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we audit three models,
Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and MiniMax M3.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/unified_domain_exposure_right_panel_new.svg" id="S3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/219;" width="381" height="219"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Exposure attribution across ten challenge phenomena.
Bars are normalized within each model–phenomenon pair.
<em id="S3.F8.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Blocked</em> segments are placed at the left to emphasize where agents reach
the intended challenge and fail because of it.
<em id="S3.F8.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Handled</em> means the agent reaches and handles the phenomenon mechanism;
<em id="S3.F8.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Untested</em> includes trajectories that never diagnose the mechanism.
Appendix <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Challenge Exposure Attribution Details ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a> gives representative
examples; Appendix <a href="#A7.SS4" title="G.4 Raw Challenge-Phenomenon Scores ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.4</span></a> reports the raw
model-by-phenomenon scores.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The per-phenomenon results reveal two patterns.</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">All current agents are weak at recovering and maintaining hidden
state.</span>
The lowest-scoring phenomena are those that demand state the instruction does
not provide directly, namely Implicit-state Inference, Multi-item State Tracking,
Conflict Disambiguation, and Dynamic Environment.
Agents cannot reliably recover information that is never stated, track it across
many items, reconcile conflicting sources, or keep it current as the task
evolves.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visual versus interaction capability separates the two frontier
models.</span>
The per-phenomenon scores expose opposite capability profiles for the two
strongest models (Table <a href="#A7.T23" title="Table 23 ‣ G.4 Raw Challenge-Phenomenon Scores ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>, partial score).
GPT-5.5 is stronger on the visual and media phenomena, Visual-spatial Precision
(51.2 vs. 43.9) and Multimodal Editing (47.0 vs. 44.0), while Opus 4.7 is
stronger where the challenge is interaction judgment rather than visual or media
output, most clearly Proactive Interaction (52.0 vs. 43.1, knowing when to
pause and ask the user).
Dynamic Environment is comparable across the two (45.1 vs. 46.2).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Analysis</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Agent Behavior</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having examined how agents fail, we now characterize the solution styles
they adopt and how those styles turn partial progress into completion.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Solution Strategies</h4>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Across the 108 tasks, the behavior-analysis models reached only partial progress in most cases
rather than a complete solution.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Completion rates range from 4.6% to 14.0% and partial-only rates from
50.0% to 67.6%, with a median score of 0.44 on non-zero runs.
Failures therefore arise less from doing nothing than from losing
constraints, relying on incomplete state, or failing to verify the
outcome.
The annotation protocol and full behavior tables are reported in
Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Because these profiles come from one run per model and strategy is
confounded with capability, we treat them as descriptive patterns rather
than causal comparisons.
Within this scope, the four behavior-analysis models exhibit distinct solution styles
(Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Across the 108 tasks, the behavior-analysis models reached only partial progress in most cases rather than a complete solution. ‣ 4.1.1 Solution Strategies ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).
GPT-5.5 is the most direct programmatic solver, dedicating 78% of its
budget to code, API, or file operations and excelling on tasks with
structured interfaces such as task 065, but weakening when constraints
surface only in the visible workflow.
Opus 4.7 is the most balanced, splitting its budget evenly between
programmatic and GUI actions at roughly 37% each, and preserving
interface-bound state more reliably, as in task 021.
Sonnet 4.6 is a stronger hybrid solver whose failures are typically
exactness errors rather than complete breakdowns.
MiniMax M3 also mixes the two modes but has the highest churn rate
among the four at 24%, leaving 45% of its runs at zero score.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Committing to one consistent solution style produces fewer
outright failures, whereas wavering between programmatic and GUI styles
is itself a failure mode.</span>
Models with a committed style, programmatic in GPT-5.5 or balanced in
Opus 4.7, achieve the lowest zero-score rates of 19% and 31%, whereas
the highest-churn system also has the highest zero-score rate,
suggesting that an unresolved choice between styles is itself a failure
mode.
Task structure further mediates this effect: task 100 succeeds under
either GUI operation or direct state editing because the underlying
state is recoverable, while tasks 003 and 010 require exact final state
or format and penalize styles that omit verification, corresponding to
the failure modes in Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/model_outcome_strategy_side_by_side_morandi.svg" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/170;" width="476" height="170"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Task outcome shares (left) and strategy mode shares (right) for each
model across the 108 evaluation tasks.
Completion rates range from 3% to 14%, with partial progress the dominant
outcome for all models.
GPT-5.5 is the most programmatic solver at 78% Code/API/file, while Opus 4.7
balances Code/API/file and GUI equally at 37% each.
MiniMax M3 and Qwen 3.7-Plus show the highest churn rates at 24% and 18%, which
coincide with the highest zero-score rates.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Action Patterns</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory-level styles above are produced by lower-level action
choices, and we now zoom in on the action budget that generates them.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/perfect_match_v2.png" id="S4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/182;" width="476" height="182" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Distribution of action budget across fifteen fine-grained
activity categories for the five evaluated models, grouped into
reasoning, perception, action, and correction phases.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.1.2 Action Patterns ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> summarizes how the
systems spend their budget across activity
categories, grouped into reasoning, perception, action, and correction
. Further perspectives are deferred to the appendix.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents spend most of their budget understanding the task.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In fixed five-step windows, the most common activities are visual
grounding (15.5%), tool-semantics reasoning (13.8%), and information
extraction (12.8%), all outranking execution (10.1%) and verification
(9.8%).
At the action level, GUI clicks (27.4%), terminal commands (24.7%),
hotkeys (14.0%), and waiting (13.9%) together account for 80.0% of
all actions, so much of the budget is spent on idle or low-leverage
steps.
Across every model, the curves in
Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.1.2 Action Patterns ‣ 4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> peak in the
perception and tool-semantics regions and decline sharply on either
side, matching the perception and domain-semantics failures of
Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Every model spends almost none of its budget on detecting and
fixing its own mistakes.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The correction phase, comprising recovery, repair, repeat-churn, goal
drift, and resource-budget pressure, occupies only a small fraction of
the budget for every model.
Recovery and repair together stay below 7% across systems: Opus 4.7
spends under 2% on recovery and roughly 3% on repair, GPT-5.5 and
Sonnet 4.6 allocate close to 3% to each, and even MiniMax M3, the
highest on this dimension, keeps both below 5%.
Repeat churn and goal drift almost never exceed 2% per category, so
agents devote almost no explicit budget to repairing earlier mistakes
even though such mistakes drive the failure modes of
Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.
This gap marks a clear lever for future progress: more visible
monitoring and self-repair should yield outsized gains on long-horizon
tasks where current systems most often stall in partial-progress states.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Agent Safety Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test whether agents actively protect user safety, we implemented “side-effect” checks (detailed in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Safety Result Details ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>) for a subset of tasks in <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>. These checks reveal that while highly capable models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 can make meaningful progress on realistic, long-horizon tasks, they often lack active concern for user safety, resulting in harmful side effects during execution. For instance, an agent might successfully push a repository to GitLab but unknowingly leak a hard-coded API key located in a project’s <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.env</span> file, as shown in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS4.SSS1" title="H.4.1 Task 026: Credential Leak ‣ H.4 Safety Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.4.1</span></a>. In another example regarding resource management, an agent notices the system has only about 398MB of disk space remaining, yet it still chooses to download 372MB of audio files for a mixing task. This completely exhausts the storage to zero, risking a system crash just to push the task forward. These findings indicate that current agents prioritize visible task completion, failing to proactively monitor their side effects.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the side-effect checks, our analysis of the trajectory data from GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.7 reveals another concerning pattern: when agents encounter obstacles or unexpected difficulties during normal interaction, they tend to use aggressive or out-of-bounds methods to force task completion. As detailed and quantified in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Safety Result Details ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>, across the 216 evaluated task trajectories (108 tasks per model), this primarily manifests as extracting hidden application states (about 14% of tasks) or bypassing user-visible interfaces (about 33% of tasks). For example, instead of gathering information properly through the UI, an agent might use browser APIs to directly extract internal application states, as illustrated by the UI-bypass case in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS4.SSS2" title="H.4.2 Task 052: UI Bypass ‣ H.4 Safety Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.4.2</span></a>. In another instance, when facing an unexpected prompt, an agent repeatedly killed the LibreOffice application and ignored document recovery warnings just to push the task forward, as shown in Appendix <a href="#A8.SS4.SSS3" title="H.4.3 Task 092: Recovery Discard ‣ H.4 Safety Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.4.3</span></a>. These cases show that agents can trigger safety issues when encountering obstacles in complex, long-horizon tasks. Although they can make partial progress, they do not handle temporary obstacles like a careful human assistant. Instead of pausing or asking the user for help when stuck, these agents attempt to escalate their privileges and do whatever it takes to finish the task. These bypass behaviors can pose unintended risks to user privacy, information security, and ongoing workflows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Ultimately, our analysis shows that realistic, long-horizon tasks expose hidden safety risks that rarely appear in simple settings. Developing a trustworthy computer-use agent that can effectively solve real-world tasks without disrupting user workflows remains a critical open challenge for future research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Human vs. Model Difficulty Gap</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Empirical agent difficulty broadly tracks human-predicted
difficulty, except on tasks humans find easy, where perceptual and
interactive demands keep most workflows hard for agents.
Each <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> task is annotated with an estimated completion time for a
skilled human user, recorded by the two annotators who timed it
(Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
We use this time as a proxy for human difficulty, grouped into three levels:
<em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Easy</em> (below 30 minutes), <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Medium</em> (30 minutes to 2 hours), and
<em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Hard</em> (above 2 hours).
Agent difficulty is defined analogously from each task’s mean partial score
across the five evaluated models, with thresholds <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Easy</em> (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;0.7</annotation></semantics></math>),
<em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Medium</em> (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.3</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7</annotation></semantics></math>), and <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Hard</em> (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.3</annotation></semantics></math>); these thresholds
are illustrative rather than prescriptive.
Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.3 Human vs. Model Difficulty Gap ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reports the row-normalized
joint distribution of human and agent difficulty (left) and of human
difficulty against the mean number of steps consumed by the agents (right).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/human_difficulty_paired_heatmaps.png" id="S4.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/181;" width="476" height="181" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>
Human-predicted difficulty against empirical agent difficulty (left) and
mean step usage (right), with rows normalized to 100%.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The left panel shows that empirical agent difficulty broadly tracks
human-predicted difficulty: 76.3% of human-hard tasks are also hard for
agents, and the share of agent-hard outcomes decreases monotonically as
human difficulty drops, from 76.3% (Hard) to 57.4% (Medium) and 44.4%
(Easy).
The one deviation appears on the human-easy side, where only 11.1% of
tasks are also easy for agents while 44.4% remain hard and another 44.4%
are medium.
This deviation is concentrated in the challenge phenomena of
Section <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS2" title="2.2.2 Challenge Phenomena ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2.2</span></a>: a human effortlessly closes a
moving pop-up in a Streaming Interaction task or visually verifies the
output of a Multimodal Editing task, whereas an agent acting from sparse
screenshots can do neither reliably.
For agents, difficulty therefore reflects what a task <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">demands</em> as
well as how long it takes, with short, routine workflows remaining hard
whenever they require tight perception-action timing or multimodal
verification, the same demands that drive the failure modes in
Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This pattern does not align with the time-horizon findings
of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwa et al. [2026]</a></cite>, where agent success on software engineering
tasks scales primarily with human completion time.
On <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, the mean step budget consumed by agents does scale with
human-estimated duration: the 0–150 step bin shrinks from 20.8% on
human-easy tasks to 0% on human-hard tasks, while the 301–450 step bin
grows from 18.9% to 42.9%.
Effort therefore scales with human time as one might predict from such a
horizon-based view, but outcome does not fully follow, since
perceptual and interactive demands also shape the success-rate gap.
This suggests that time-horizon trends established on software tasks
transfer only partially to general computer-use settings, where progress
will require advances along axes orthogonal to horizon length.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px7" title="Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier models have opposite capability profiles. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> identifies <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> agents score low;
this section examines <em id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> they fail.
We inspected trajectories from all evaluated models, focusing on information
flow and execution patterns.
Rather than lacking the basic ability to perform GUI actions or write code,
agents mainly fail in long-horizon tasks along five recurring dimensions:
information grounding and tracking, perception–action timing, domain knowledge
and workflow learning, verification and reflection, and long-horizon state
drift.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents miss information from the instruction, the environment, or the user channel.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The failure is usually not that the needed information is entirely absent.
Agents may lose explicit instruction constraints, such as required file formats
or naming rules, overlook information revealed during execution, or proceed
under missing evidence when they should ask the user.
In the purchase-order task
(Task 035; Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, top row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS2" title="H.2.2 Task 035: Dynamic Environment ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.2</span></a>), a new TeamChat message overrides
an earlier rule while the agent is reading another request, and a later
correction changes the budget and vendor constraints again.
The failure is not a missing click; it is stale grounding.
The agent treats communication as background noise instead of updating the
task state.
When required information is absent, agents show the same weakness in another
form: in the DS-2019 task
(Task 024; Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS3" title="H.2.3 Task 024: Proactive Interaction ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.3</span></a>), weaker trajectories
submit incomplete applications instead of using <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ASK_USER</span> to request
missing financial evidence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents fail on time-sensitive tasks when long observation-to-action gaps make their actions target stale interface states.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In streaming interfaces, the agent can correctly reason about the observed
screenshot, but the screen changes before the action is executed.
In the TravelHub booking task
(Task 052; Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, middle row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS1" title="H.2.1 Task 052: Streaming Interaction ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.1</span></a>), a promotional pop-up moves
continuously while the agent is deciding what to do.
The close button is visible in the screenshot, but by the time the click is
issued the pop-up has shifted to a new location.
The resulting action is stale: it targets the old coordinate rather than the
current UI state.
This is not a semantic misunderstanding of the page; it is a timing failure in
the discrete observe–think–act loop used by screenshot-based agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents struggle with interpreting and generating domain-specific artifacts.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The agent must understand the artifact’s domain semantics, choose a useful
representation, and follow a workflow that can produce a valid
output.
In the FreeCAD reconstruction task
(Task 103; Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, bottom row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS2" title="H.1.2 Task 103: FreeCAD Reconstruction ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.2</span></a>), agents read dimensions from an
engineering drawing and generate a plausible support bracket, but do not keep a
stable mapping from features to dimensions, primitives, and geometric checks.
The final model looks reasonable but fails on exact geometry.
A similar pattern appears in video editing
(Task 055; Appendix <a href="#A8.SS3.SSS1" title="H.3.1 Task 055: Video Tutorial ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.1</span></a>), where agents infer
an edit from static keyframes and simple <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ffmpeg</span> operations, but lose
the timeline structure and transition timing that define the target artifact.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents often fail to verify task-critical properties and correct errors they have already noticed before submission.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Completing a visible action is not the same as checking whether the result
satisfies the task.
Agents may observe an output or even notice a problem, but that observation does
not reliably change the plan.
In the reimbursement task
(Task 008; Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS1" title="H.1.1 Task 008: Expense Reimbursement ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.1</span></a>), the agent reads the
account-code rules, cross-checks bank charges, and submits the report.
However, submission is not verification: the final state can still contain wrong
fields, missing details, or incomplete supporting documents.
Task 035 shows the same failure in a dynamic setting.
Once an early purchase-order decision becomes part of the working plan, later
evidence often fails to trigger a full repair.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agents forget information gathered early when task state is stored only in compressed reasoning or chain-of-thought context.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Long tasks require the agent to preserve constraints, evidence, intermediate
decisions, and verification targets over hundreds of steps.
Current agents often store this state only in compressed reasoning or
chain-of-thought context.
As a result, information gathered early can disappear by the time the final
artifact is produced.
For instance, Task 008 loses precise reimbursement details across applications.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The clearest contrast appears in paired trajectories.
GPT-5.5 often turns a desktop workflow into direct manipulation of a lower-level
representation, such as DOM state, APIs, OOXML, or generated media.
This can be efficient, but it is brittle when success depends on the
application-level artifact.
In Task 035 (Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, top row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS2.SSS2" title="H.2.2 Task 035: Dynamic Environment ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.2</span></a>), it edits the workbook XML directly
and overwrites the protected row instead of appending approved purchases.
The same pattern appears in Task 058
(Appendix <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Challenge Exposure Attribution Details ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a>), where a WPS Morph task
becomes rendered frames, in Task 055
(Appendix <a href="#A8.SS3.SSS1" title="H.3.1 Task 055: Video Tutorial ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.1</span></a>), where video similarity
substitutes for the MLT timeline, and in Task 103
(Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, bottom row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS2" title="H.1.2 Task 103: FreeCAD Reconstruction ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.2</span></a>), where a plausible STEP export still
has incorrect geometry.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Claude Opus 4.7 stays closer to the visible interface.
Its failures therefore look less like direct-state substitution and more like
persistent work that does not converge.
In Task 035, it preserves the workbook contract but misses Emily’s Salesforce
approval.
In Task 008 (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS1" title="H.1.1 Task 008: Expense Reimbursement ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.1</span></a>), it carries much of
the reimbursement evidence through a long GUI workflow, but exact per-diem and
attachment details drift before submission.
Task 058 (Appendix <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Challenge Exposure Attribution Details ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a>) shows the same
pattern in WPS, where manual search and editing end in approximate picture
objects rather than the required Morph construction.
In Task 055 (Appendix <a href="#A8.SS3.SSS1" title="H.3.1 Task 055: Video Tutorial ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.1</span></a>) and Task 103
(Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 fail in different ways. ‣ 4.4 Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, bottom row;
Appendix <a href="#A8.SS1.SSS2" title="H.1.2 Task 103: FreeCAD Reconstruction ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1.2</span></a>), continued tool-level repair creates
partial timeline or geometry structure, but not the invariants needed for full
success.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/failure_mode_demonstration_035_052_103.png" id="S4.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/334;" width="476" height="334" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>
Representative failure modes in <span id="S4.F12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
Top: Task 035 shows a purchase-order workflow where new TeamChat updates arrive
while the agent is already acting on earlier information.
Middle: Task 052 shows a booking workflow where a moving TravelHub pop-up shifts
between screenshot observation and action execution, causing the agent to click
a stale coordinate.
Bottom: Task 103 shows a FreeCAD workflow where the agent reads an engineering drawing
and builds a plausible model, but the geometry remains incorrect.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agentic evaluation has evolved from domain-specific executable benchmarks toward
harder, longer, and more realistic work. SWE-bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>]</cite>
made real GitHub issue resolution a software-engineering testbed, and
WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>]</cite> placed web agents in reproducible everyday
websites, while OSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>]</cite> established open-ended desktop
computer use in real operating-system environments. The deployment of
general-purpose agents such as Claude Cowork <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026a</a>]</cite>,
OpenAI Codex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025b</a>]</cite>, and OpenClaw <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenClaw Contributors, 2026</a>]</cite> further
shifted evaluation toward delegated workflows across files, applications, tools,
and communication channels. Recent benchmarks then raise difficulty, horizon
length, or economic realism: SWE-Bench Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2025</a>]</cite>
for enterprise-like software engineering,
Terminal-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill et al., 2026</a>]</cite> for
command-line workflows, METR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwa et al., 2026</a>]</cite> for
human-time task horizons, ProgramBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>]</cite> for
whole-program reconstruction,
GDPval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patwardhan et al., 2025</a>]</cite> for professional
deliverables, and APEX-Agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vidgen et al., 2026</a>]</cite> for high-value
cross-application knowledge work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-use evaluation has developed in parallel from general desktop control
toward more diverse, stateful, and domain-rich settings.
MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>]</cite> focuses on personalized computer state,
but its reported trajectories remain much shorter than the multi-hundred-step
workflows studied here. Orion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2026</a>]</cite> targets scientific computer
use and lab automation, while Agents’ Last
Exam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2026</a>]</cite> grounds long tasks in verifiable professional tasks, but only a small fraction exercise GUI-based computer use,
and it lacks systematic coverage of dynamic environments, proactive user
interaction, and other phenomena central to realistic computer use.
These benchmarks capture important slices of
agentic work, but none jointly tests long-horizon GUI operation,
multi-application coordination, dynamic state changes, user interaction, complex
tutorial following, multimodal editing, stateful personal context, and
safety-sensitive execution.
<span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> targets this missing intersection, combining all three dimensions: tasks that run over long horizons, unfold on a realistic desktop spanning many applications, and directly stress these phenomena.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> covers a broad set of realistic long-horizon computer-use workflows,
but it is not meant to exhaust the full space of professional computer use.
Some domains and occupations are necessarily underrepresented, because complex
professional workflows differ in how reliably they can be recreated, hosted, and
evaluated. Challenge-phenomenon and occupational-domain results should therefore
be interpreted as diagnostic rather than comprehensive. We view <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> as a
foundation for an extended <span id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> series, and future extensions will add
more domains, occupations, and workflow types while preserving the same release discipline and comparable evaluation principles.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Scaling the benchmark remains costly. Each task requires realistic artifacts,
reproducible environments, robust scoring logic, and human- and model-based
quality control. Aggregate scores may also depend on the current task mix and
on stochastic agent behavior. As with other
reproducible benchmarks, agents may also learn to exploit benchmark-specific
artifacts in self-hosted environments over time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> evaluates computer-use agents in a setting that existing benchmarks
do not fully capture: realistic, complex, long-horizon workflows grounded in
authentic artifacts and stateful workspace data.
It contains 108 end-to-end tasks spanning everyday and professional work, and
targets challenge phenomena that are common in real workflows, including dynamic
environments, streaming interaction, proactive interaction, cross-source
reasoning, implicit-state inference, and visual-spatial or multimodal
verification.
Its self-hosted services, fine-grained partial rewards, validated model-based
checks, versioned releases, and safety audits support reproducible comparison.
Our experiments show that current agents remain far from reliable computer use:
the strongest setting, Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking and batched tool
calls, reaches only 20.6% binary accuracy and 54.8% partial-score accuracy.
Performance drops sharply as tasks grow longer, and agents struggle most when
they must recover hidden state, track many items, resolve conflicting
information, or adapt to changing requirements.
These findings show that progress requires agents that can maintain task state,
monitor evolving environments, verify final artifacts, and repair errors across
long workflows.
<span id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> provides a basis for measuring that progress.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Additional Related Benchmarks and Computer-Use Foundations</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The broader agent-evaluation landscape includes earlier web and browser-control
settings such as World of Bits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2017</a>]</cite>,
MiniWoB++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Farama Foundation, 2023</a>]</cite>,
WebShop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>]</cite>, and
WebLINX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>]</cite>, as well as web-agent benchmarks and ecosystems
such as Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>]</cite>,
Online-Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xue et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
VisualWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
WebVoyager <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
WorkArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
AssistantBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
WebChoreArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miyai et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
BrowseComp <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>]</cite>, and
BrowserGym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chezelles et al., 2025</a>]</cite>.
Desktop, OS, and mobile computer-use benchmarks include
OmniAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2024a</a>]</cite>,
WONDERBREAD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wornow et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
OSWorld-MCP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jia et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
Computer Agent Arena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026b</a>]</cite>,
Windows Agent Arena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
WorldGUI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
OS-MAP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
OS-Marathon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>]</cite>,
WindowsWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026a</a>]</cite>,
MacOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025c</a>]</cite>,
MyPCBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026a</a>]</cite>,
Android in the Wild <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2023</a>]</cite>,
AndroidWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
AndroidLab <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024b</a>]</cite>,
Android Agent Arena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chai et al., 2026</a>]</cite>,
AndroidControl-Curated <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leung et al., 2025</a>]</cite>,
MobileBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
MobileWorldBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>]</cite>,
MobileWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kong et al., 2025</a>]</cite>, and
iOSWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2026b</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Complementary GUI-agent and computer-use foundation work includes
RCI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>]</cite>,
Pix2Act <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shaw et al., 2023</a>]</cite>,
AppAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>]</cite>,
SeeAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
SeeClick <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>]</cite>,
ScreenSpot-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>]</cite>,

Agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025a</a>]</cite> and Gemini Computer
Use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2025</a>]</cite>, further motivate evaluation beyond
single-application or short-horizon computer-control tasks.</p>

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Environments, Applications, and Assets</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Self-hosted Websites</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.1 Self-hosted Websites ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> lists general-purpose self-hosted websites, covering widely used web services that are reusable across multiple tasks.
Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ C.1 Self-hosted Websites ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> lists task-specific websites, each built for an individual workflow.
Except for self-deployable applications such as Moodle and GitLab, all websites are renamed from their real-world counterparts to prevent agent
confusion (e.g., an agent navigating to the real Gmail after closing a tab)
and to avoid trademark or phishing concerns.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Website Framework</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ C.2 Website Framework ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> summarizes the architecture
of the <span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> self-hosted website framework.
The framework provides controlled, reproducible web environments for the
websites that carry task-relevant information, avoiding evaluation noise from
changing page layouts, account-specific histories, anti-bot defenses,
production-side data pollution, and non-deterministic reset behavior, while
the agent retains full access to the open web for search and browsing.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.29537v2/self_hosted_website.svg" id="A3.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Overview of the <span id="A3.F13.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> self-hosted website framework.
Annotators inspect documentation, edit state JSON, and export initial states;
the initial state is routed to self-hosted web applications; the browser agent
interacts with the web interface; the evaluator scores the final state and
uploaded files.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">OSWorld-web organizes websites as independent application directories that can
be composed into a shared deployment.
Each application exposes its web service on an internal port and provides a
<span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">web-compose.yml</span> file.
A Caddy reverse proxy routes domain names such as <span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">appname.localhost</span>
or <span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">appname.HOST_SUFFIX</span> to the corresponding container, while all
applications share the same Docker network.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">basesite</span> implementation provides the common scaffold: a unified
Next.js application with both frontend pages and backend API routes.
The backend exposes standardized experiment interfaces: <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/api/state</span> for
state lifecycle operations, <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/api/files</span> for user-scoped file uploads
and downloads, <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/api/info</span> for runtime information, and <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/health</span>
for service checks.
A <span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/state-manage</span> page enables task authors to read the state schema,
inspect and edit the current cookie-scoped state, save a new state, reset the
environment, and download the edited JSON.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">State is represented as a JSON envelope with metadata and task data.
Identity is scoped by a browser cookie named <span id="A3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">user_id</span>, allowing
multiple agents or task instances to use the same web application concurrently
without contaminating one another’s state.
Files are handled through the same isolation mechanism: uploaded artifacts are
stored under the current user identity and can be removed together with the
state on reset.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">During evaluation, task setup writes the required initial JSON state and
launches the application container.
The agent interacts only through the browser-facing interface, as a normal
user would.
At the end of the trajectory, the evaluator reads the final state and
associated uploads and applies task-specific scoring checkpoints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Desktop Applications</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ C.3 Desktop Applications ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> lists the desktop applications used as primary
task environments in <span id="A3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>.
Each entry corresponds to an application that at least one task requires by
instruction or setup; general-purpose utilities such as file managers and
terminal emulators are excluded.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T8" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Application Coverage Analysis</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ C.4 Application Coverage Analysis ‣ Appendix C Environments, Applications, and Assets ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> counts, for each application or self-hosted
website, how many tasks <em id="A3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">require</em> it—meaning the app is explicitly
named in the task instruction or launched by the task setup, and the task
cannot be completed without it.
This is the <em id="A3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">definite</em> count from §<a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>; it
does not include apps that agents happened to use as optional auxiliary
tools during rollout execution (the <em id="A3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">possibly involved</em> count).
The two counts differ substantially: for example, VS Code appears in 9
tasks as a required app, but agent rollouts invoke it in additional tasks
as an optional scripting tool.
The distribution is strongly long-tailed: a small set of general-purpose
tools recur across many tasks, while most domain-specific applications appear
in only one or two tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Chrome dominates as the primary browser interface, appearing in 62 of 108
tasks; it serves both as a vehicle for self-hosted websites and as a
standalone tool for web-based workflows.
Among self-hosted websites, MailHub and TeamChat are most frequently required,
reflecting the prominence of email and team communication workflows.
On the desktop side, LibreOffice Writer and WPS Presentation are the
highest-frequency applications, followed by VS Code and Shotcut.
Most specialised tools—3D CAD packages, domain-specific scientific
software, and robotics simulators—appear in only one to three tasks each,
but collectively account for a large share of the unique expertise the
benchmark demands.
This long-tail structure ensures breadth of domain coverage while keeping
individual task workflows realistic and deep rather than superficially broad.</p>
</div>
