</section>
<section id="A3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.5 </span>Challenge Phenomena Descriptions</h3>

<div id="A3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The following paragraphs provide detailed descriptions and illustrative examples
for each of the ten challenge phenomena introduced in
Section <a href="#S2.SS2.SSS2" title="2.2.2 Challenge Phenomena ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T10" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>Full definitions of challenge phenomena in <span id="A3.T10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>. Tags are
non-exclusive; a task may belong to multiple phenomena, and percentages sum to
more than 100%.</figcaption>
<table id="A3.T10.4" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<th id="A3.T10.4.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A3.T10.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phenomenon</span></th>
<th id="A3.T10.4.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A3.T10.4.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"># Tasks (%)</span></th>

<span id="A3.T10.4.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T10.4.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Brief definition</span></span>

<tr id="A3.T10.4.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T10.4.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">Cross-source Reasoning</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">46 (42.6%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.2.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Reconciling task-relevant facts across multiple independent sources, such as
emails, documents, websites, records, or prior messages.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T10.4.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">Visual-spatial Precision</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">45 (41.7%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.3.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Executing tasks that require precise visual localization, geometry, placement,
timing, alignment, or pixel-/layout-level verification.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T10.4.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">Implicit-state Inference</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">43 (39.8%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.4.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Inferring required state that is not stated in the instruction and is not
available from a single obvious source, such as prior submissions, logs, saved

</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T10.4.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">Multi-item State Tracking</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">43 (39.8%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Maintaining correct state across a large set of structured items, such as rows,
records, events, candidates, annotations, or document edits.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.6" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T10.4.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.6.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Resolving stale, noisy, contradictory, or distracting information by identifying
which source is authoritative and which should be ignored or overridden.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.7" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T10.4.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">30 (27.8%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.7.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.7.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Producing, modifying, or verifying substantive non-text media artifacts,
including images, video, audio, CAD/3D objects, or medical-image segmentations.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T10.4.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">Tutorial Following</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">22 (20.4%)</td>
<td id="A3.T10.4.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.8.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.8.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Extracting procedures from external guidance, such as PDF/web guides, video
walkthroughs, or prior completed work, and adapting them to the current task.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.9" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T10.4.9.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.9.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.9.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Revising plans when new task-relevant information arrives during execution, such
as emails or team-chat messages that change requirements.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.10" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T10.4.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">

<span id="A3.T10.4.10.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Acting in environments whose visual state changes between observation and action,
making discrete screenshot-based interaction insufficient.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T10.4.11" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A3.T10.4.11.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="A3.T10.4.11.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="A3.T10.4.11.3.1.1" class="ltx_p">Detecting incomplete, ambiguous, or invalid task conditions and proactively
asking the simulated user for clarification or additional evidence before
proceeding.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Streaming Interaction.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Current agents observe the screen as a discrete sequence of screenshots and
produce actions at each step without any streaming input or output.
Because the environment can change continuously between the moment the agent
takes a screenshot and the moment it executes an action, the visual state at
action time may differ from the state the agent reasoned about.
Some tasks are therefore structurally impossible for current screenshot-based
frameworks: the agent may correctly identify a target element’s position in the
observed screenshot, yet the element has moved by the time the click is
executed.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In a TravelHub hotel booking task (§<a href="#A8.SS2.SSS1" title="H.2.1 Task 052: Streaming Interaction ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.1</span></a>),
a promotional popup appears at a random position on screen and must be closed
before the booking can proceed.
Because the popup continues to animate after each observation, the agent’s
computed click coordinate is consistently offset from the popup’s actual
position at action time, and the close button cannot be reliably hit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dynamic Environment.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In some tasks, new information arrives through communication channels
(such as messages in a TeamChat channel or emails) while the agent is
executing, changing or extending the requirements mid-workflow.
The agent’s initial plan, formed on the basis of the environment’s state at
task start, may no longer be correct after these updates; the agent must
perceive the changes and revise its strategy accordingly.
This is distinct from Streaming Interaction: the challenge is not perceptual
timing but planning coherence under evolving goals.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In a purchase-order task (§<a href="#A8.SS2.SSS2" title="H.2.2 Task 035: Dynamic Environment ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.2</span></a>), the manager posts budget rules
and vendor restrictions in a TeamChat channel at task start; during execution,
new messages arrive that introduce a special exception for one item, and later
a major correction that raises the hardware budget cap and changes the approved
vendor.
An agent that commits to its initial plan and does not monitor the channel will
produce an incorrect form, even if every individual action is executed
correctly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tutorial Following.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many real computer-use tasks require consulting external guidance before or
during execution, and translating that guidance into GUI operations on
potentially different inputs.
Tutorial-derived data has been useful for scaling GUI-agent supervision, as in
AgentTrek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024c</a>]</cite> and
VideoAgentTrek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>]</cite>; in
<span id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span>, however, tutorials are part of the task evidence that an evaluated
agent must interpret during execution.
<span id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> captures three forms of tutorial that arise in real professional
workflows: written PDF or web guides (e.g., a DS-160 visa application guide);
video walkthroughs (e.g., a Shotcut editing tutorial hosted on StreamView); and
prior completed work used as a style or format template (e.g., existing
presentation slides whose formatting new slides must match).
The challenge in each case is not following a script but extracting the
relevant procedure from a heterogeneous source and adapting it to the current
task inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The video form is the most difficult for current agents (§<a href="#A8.SS3.SSS1" title="H.3.1 Task 055: Video Tutorial ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.1</span></a>).
When the reference is a video, the agent cannot read it sequentially like text;
current multimodal agents process video by extracting discrete keyframes, which
discards temporal information such as transition duration, animation speed, and
playback timing.
As a result, the agent may correctly identify <em id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what</em> elements appear in
the video but fail to reproduce <em id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> they are animated or sequenced.
The PDF/web guide variant (§<a href="#A8.SS3.SSS2" title="H.3.2 Task 098: PDF/Web Guide Tutorial ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.2</span></a>)
requires the agent to alternate between a structured guide tab and a live form,
mapping each instruction to the correct field while handling conditional entries
described only in the guide.
The template variant (§<a href="#A8.SS3.SSS3" title="H.3.3 Task 004: Previous Work as Template ‣ H.3 Tutorial-Following Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3.3</span></a>)
provides no written guide at all: the agent must inspect existing slides, infer
the formatting rules (font, master slide, layout, colour scheme), and apply
them to new slides.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Proactive Interaction.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some tasks involve instructions or environments that are incomplete, ambiguous,
or contain invalid information that the agent cannot resolve from the
environment alone.
Rather than proceeding under false assumptions, the agent must independently
detect the problem and proactively contact the simulated user—requesting
additional documents, flagging inconsistencies, or asking targeted questions
before proceeding.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In a DS-2019 visa application task (§<a href="#A8.SS2.SSS3" title="H.2.3 Task 024: Proactive Interaction ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.3</span></a>), the agent fills nine
questionnaires and then detects that the financial certificate on file shows
only $12,000 while the required program cost is $18,000.
Instead of submitting and risking rejection, it stops, summarizes the shortfall,
and requests an updated certificate via <span id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ASK_USER</span>.
When the user provides a new certificate, the agent scrutinizes its metadata,
detects suspicious inconsistencies, and raises further concerns before
continuing.
This phenomenon tests whether agents can identify information gaps or errors,
avoid acting under insufficient conditions, and initiate appropriately targeted
interactions with a human collaborator.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multimodal Editing.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a narrow definition of multimodal editing in this paper. The tag covers
tasks that require producing, modifying, or verifying substantive non-text media
artifacts, including image editing, video or audio editing, 3D rendering or CAD
reconstruction, and medical-image segmentation.
It does not include tasks whose visual component is limited to presentation
rendering or reading scanned/image-based PDFs, without substantive creation or
editing of a non-text media artifact.
These tasks stress perceptual grounding across modalities and output
verification capabilities that go beyond standard GUI navigation: the agent
must not only operate the correct software tools but also judge whether the
result matches the intended specification.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Critically, multimodal editing tasks test <em id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">visual understanding</em>, not
only software proficiency.
An agent that knows how to use video editing software cannot succeed without
first understanding what it is looking for visually.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">One task asks the agent to locate all spider sprites across frames of a game
video and replace them with solid black regions while preserving the original
video duration and frame rate (§<a href="#A8.SS2.SSS4" title="H.2.4 Task 053: Multimodal Editing ‣ H.2 Challenge-Phenomenon Case Studies ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.2.4</span></a>).
This is a Hogwarts Legacy gameplay clip in which “spiders” are large
arthropod enemy creatures with distinct visual appearances: not simple
geometric icons.
Answering the question <em id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what does a spider look like in this video?</em>
requires semantic visual comprehension of the game domain, independent of any
tool-use skill.
Success therefore requires parsing video frames, identifying targets by their
visual appearance across varying poses and lighting conditions, applying
spatial edits precisely, and verifying the output meets both the content and
format constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-source Reasoning.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many tasks require reconciling task-relevant facts across multiple independent
sources rather than copying information from a single page.
Examples include matching a bank transaction to an email receipt and policy
document, combining course requirements from a PDF and a scheduling system, or
checking a candidate profile against attachments, web links, and prior
messages.
This phenomenon tests whether the agent can identify authoritative sources, carry
facts across applications, and ensure that the final action is consistent with
all of them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Visual-spatial Precision.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This phenomenon captures tasks whose success depends on precise visual
localization, geometry, timing, placement, or media alignment.
It is broader than Multimodal Editing: a task may require exact spatial
positioning or visual comparison without producing a new media artifact.
These tasks stress pixel- and layout-level grounding, object placement,
segmentation boundaries, frame timing, and visual verification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implicit-state Inference.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some required information is not stated in the user instruction and is not
available from a single obvious source.
The agent must infer where the missing state should live, such as a prior
submitted form, an application database, a saved log, a hidden environment
state, or a runtime artifact produced by the workflow.
This phenomenon distinguishes tasks that require task-consistent inference of
latent state from tasks where all necessary facts are explicitly provided.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px9" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-item State Tracking.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real workflows often require maintaining correct state across a large set of
structured items: purchase-order rows, calendar events, reimbursement lines,
candidate records, annotations, or document edits.
Errors arise when an agent handles a few items correctly but loses consistency
across the batch, applies a rule to only some records, duplicates work, or
forgets exceptions encountered earlier.
This phenomenon therefore measures state maintenance across many structured items,
not merely task length.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px10" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Conflict Disambiguation.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px10.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS5.SSS0.Px10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In realistic environments, sources may be stale, noisy, inconsistent, or
deliberately distracting.
The agent must decide which information is authoritative and which should be
ignored or overridden.
This includes resolving contradictory messages, distinguishing final updates
from superseded instructions, filtering distractor records, and avoiding
plausible but invalid evidence.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.6 </span>Benchmark Releases</h3>

<div id="A3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reliable comparison also requires controlling benchmark updates after release.
Task fixes, website updates, OSWorld code changes, task dataset changes, and
provider image changes can all affect agent scores, so results should only be
compared within the same official benchmark release.
<span id="A3.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> therefore uses compact release manifests, documented in
<span id="A3.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">benchmark_releases/README.md</span>, to define each comparable release by its
task dataset tag, website code tag, OSWorld code tag, task hash manifest, and
provider-specific Ubuntu image definitions.
The experiments in this paper use release <span id="A3.SS6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">v2026.06.24</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When a release needs a correction, we create new immutable tags and a new
manifest rather than editing the previous release.
Each run also records detailed provenance, including the selected release, task
tag, code tag, website tag, provider, image, and verification status, so
official benchmark results can be separated from local development runs and from
results generated under later releases.
This release discipline complements open computer-use-agent foundations such as
OpenCUA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>]</cite>: beyond releasing
models or training data, evaluation artifacts must also pin task, code,
environment, and image versions to make reported scores auditable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.7 </span>Licenses for Existing Assets</h3>

<div id="A3.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> uses and extends several categories of existing assets.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prior OSWorld assets.</span>
We build on the original OSWorld benchmark, including its codebase, task
structure, evaluation assets, and file caches, released under Apache-2.0.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0<span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> task artifacts.</span></span>
Task-specific files, documents, scripts, media files, and cached assets
newly created for <span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> are author-created and released with the
<span id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> package under the project license unless otherwise noted.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agent and runner infrastructure.</span>
Some runner scripts, agent implementations, and utility functions adapt
code from WebArena, Agent-S/AgentS2, and Qwen2.5-VL utilities, all
released under Apache-2.0.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vendored or derived agent framework code.</span>
<span id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> includes or adapts AG2/AutoGen-related components and
FastDepends components governed by Apache-2.0 and MIT licenses
as applicable.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>External Interviews for Task Inspiration</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">External participants were involved only during early task ideation.
Interviews were used to collect high-level examples of realistic software
workflows, commonly used applications, typical input artifacts, task
constraints, and expected deliverables.
Participants were not asked to operate the benchmark, complete tasks, annotate
trajectories, verify rubrics, evaluate agents, provide screenshots, or share
private documents, credentials, personal data, or confidential workplace
information.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The instruction was limited to: “Please describe realistic computer-use
workflows that you or people in your role commonly perform, including the
applications involved, the input artifacts, the constraints, and the final
deliverables. Please do not share private documents, credentials, personal
data, or confidential workplace information.”
The authors used these interviews only as inspiration for benchmark task design;
no participant-provided private material appears in the released tasks,
artifacts, or evaluations.
No compensation was provided.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Because the interviews were limited to voluntary, low-risk task-ideation
conversations, we did not identify risks beyond ordinary professional
discussion.
The study underwent internal ethics review, which determined that this component
did not involve risk-bearing interventions or collection of sensitive personal
information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety</h2>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We validate the reliability of the two model-dependent components in our
evaluation framework: the model judge used for open-ended checkpoint
evaluation, and the user-simulating model used in information-seeking tasks.
This focus differs from verifiable training-environment generation such as
CUA-Gym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026a</a>]</cite>: our checkpoints are designed for benchmark
measurement and are manually audited against task goals, rather than generated
as RL training rewards.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Judge Validation.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We collect intermediate states from agent rollouts and manually add extra states
when needed, preparing three states per task from 20 tasks.
We compare judge decisions from four models (GPT-5.4 medium, GPT-5.4 xhigh,
Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) against human-annotated ground truth.
For Claude models we set temperature to 0; for GPT-5.4 models, which do not
support temperature control, we run each evaluation three times and report
the average.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report two metrics.
Checkpoint agreement treats each model-evaluated checkpoint equally:</p>
<table id="A5.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{agreement}=\frac{\text{number of correct judge decisions}}{\text{total number of judge decisions}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>agreement</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>number of correct judge decisions</mtext><mtext>total number of judge decisions</mtext></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{agreement}=\frac{\text{number of correct judge decisions}}{\text{total number of judge decisions}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Score-weighted agreement weights each checkpoint by its contribution to the
task score:</p>
<table id="A5.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{weighted agreement}=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbb{I}[\text{judge}_{i}=\text{human}_{i}]}{\sum_{i}w_{i}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>weighted agreement</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>w</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mtext>judge</mtext><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>human</mtext><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{weighted agreement}=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbb{I}[\text{judge}_{i}=\text{human}_{i}]}{\sum_{i}w_{i}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ User Simulation Validation. ‣ E.1 Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows that all judge models exceed 93%
agreement on both metrics.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 is the most robust judge, reaching 98.5% checkpoint
agreement and 98.6% score-weighted agreement.
GPT-5.4 xhigh and Claude Opus 4.6 sometimes produce stricter judgments than
human annotators, leading to slightly lower agreement.
Text-based judgments are generally more reliable than image-based judgments,
consistent with our decision to restrict model-based evaluation to objective
binary checklist items.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User Simulation Validation.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each of 20 tasks involving proactive interaction, we prepare 20
intermediate states and query each candidate user-simulating model.
Human annotators then verify whether each model response is reasonable.
Table <a href="#A5.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ User Simulation Validation. ‣ E.1 Validation of Model-Based Evaluation and User Simulation ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> shows that all models exceed 95%
human-verified accuracy; Claude Sonnet 4.6 reaches 100%, supporting its
selection as the user-simulating model.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T11" class="ltx_table">

</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Safety Result Details</h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ E.2 Safety Result Details ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> summarizes the side-effect checks used in our evaluation. These checks diagnose severe side effects that may not affect the visible task completion score.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond these checks, we also analyzed the trajectories of GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 for unsafe behaviors. As shown in Table <a href="#A5.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ E.2 Safety Result Details ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol, Validation, and Safety ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, both models extract hidden application states at similar rates. However, Claude Opus 4.7 is significantly more likely to bypass user-visible interfaces, primarily due to its tendency to make system-level environment changes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T13" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Agent Behavior Annotation Details</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix describes the behavioral annotation used in
Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Agent Behavior ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.
The behavioral annotation results were produced by GPT-5.5 with <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">xhigh</span>
reasoning effort over existing per-task structured reports.
The annotation inputs were the task instructions, trajectory summaries, observed
actions and states, final outcomes, and scoring feedback available in those
reports.
The generated annotations were further human-verified before being used in the
analysis.Table <a href="#A6.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> reports the aggregate scored outcomes
for the four behavior-analysis models, and
Table <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> summarizes the annotation standard.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The annotation separates overlapping behavior labels from mutually exclusive
primary modes.
A model-task trajectory can receive any number of behavior labels when the
corresponding behavior is meaningfully present.
In contrast, each trajectory receives exactly one primary mode, chosen as the
dominant strategy that best explains how the model attempted to solve the task.
Because GPT-5.5 trajectories include unavoidable batch tool calls, the
annotations focus on semantic behavior rather than raw call counts.Tables <a href="#A6.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> and
<a href="#A6.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> define the two taxonomies, and
Tables <a href="#A6.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> and <a href="#A6.T20" title="Table 20 ‣ Appendix F Agent Behavior Annotation Details ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>
report the corresponding per-model counts over the 108 annotated trajectories.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.T15" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 15: </span>Aggregate task outcomes for the behavior analysis models.
Claude Opus 4.7 has one missing score, task 048, so its aggregate outcome
denominator is 107 scored tasks.</figcaption>

<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The annotation standard given to GPT-5.5 was:</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.T16" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 16: </span>Annotation standard used for behavior labeling.</figcaption>

<span id="A6.T16.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Unit of annotation</span>

<td id="A6.T16.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">

</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T16.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">

</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">

<span id="A6.T16.2.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Use the task instruction, observed actions, state observations,
trajectory summary, final outcome, and scoring feedback in the structured
report.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T16.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:79.3pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Behavior labels</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:241.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Mark every behavior label that is meaningfully present.
Labels are binary and can overlap; do not treat a label as implying success.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T16.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:79.3pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Primary mode</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:241.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Select exactly one primary mode: the dominant strategy over the
full trajectory. If several strategies appear, choose the one that best explains
how the model attempted to solve the task.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T16.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">

<span id="A6.T16.2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Conservatism</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:241.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Do not assign a label for a single incidental action or
ambiguous evidence. Use <em id="A6.T16.2.6.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Other</em> as a primary mode only when the trajectory
does not fit the listed modes.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.7" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A6.T16.2.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparability</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T16.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:241.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">For GPT-5.5, ignore raw batch-call counts and annotate the
semantic behavior expressed by the calls.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T16.2.8" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A6.T16.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:79.3pt;">
<span id="A6.T16.2.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Example</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T16.2.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">

<span id="A6.T16.2.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">In a ticket-booking task, a trajectory that clicks through the seat
map while inspecting or invoking booking and payment APIs may receive Direct
code/API/file strategy, Human-style GUI strategy, and Hybrid GUI + code strategy
labels. Its primary mode is whichever mechanism carried the solution.</span>
</span></td></tr>

<span id="A6.T17.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Behavior label</span>
</span></th>
<th id="A6.T17.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt">

<span id="A6.T17.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Direct code/API/file strategy</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A6.T17.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory uses shell commands, scripts,
application APIs, DOM or session state, local storage, structured files,
databases, XML/JSON, or other programmatic state manipulation in a meaningful
attempt to solve or inspect the task.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.3" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.3.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory uses visible desktop interaction,
such as clicking, typing, menus, dragging, scrolling, or visual confirmation,

</span></td></tr>

<span id="A6.T17.2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Hybrid GUI + code strategy</span>

<span id="A6.T17.2.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory materially combines GUI actions
with programmatic inspection or modification, and both sources of action or
evidence affect the solving plan.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.5" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A6.T17.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GUI/visual grounding issue</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory misreads, misses, or cannot
reliably use visible UI state, including coordinates, layout, element identity,
current selections, visual feedback, or screen evidence, causing wrong actions
or uncertainty.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Loop/repeated recovery churn</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory repeats recovery cycles,
reselection, retries, redundant checks, resets, or strategy changes without
gaining enough new information to converge.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Planning or goal drift</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory deviates from the user instruction or
loses task-specific constraints, works on the wrong artifact or subgoal, or
follows an inconsistent plan.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Final-state exactness failure</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.8.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The final state is plausible or partially
complete but does not satisfy the specified task requirements, such as wrong
values, wrong selected items, wrong formatting, wrong file structure, or missing
saved state.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Premature stop / false done</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.9.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.9.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory stops or declares completion while
important work remains, uncertainty is unresolved, or the final state has not
been sufficiently checked.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.10.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Step/time exhaustion</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A6.T17.2.10.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.10.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The trajectory is substantially limited by step or time
budget, usually after long exploration, retries, or slow GUI progress,
preventing completion.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A6.T17.2.11" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A6.T17.2.11.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A6.T17.2.11.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:103.5pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.11.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Scoring/environment mismatch</span>
</span></td>
<td id="A6.T17.2.11.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A6.T17.2.11.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:217.4pt;">
<span id="A6.T17.2.11.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">The failure plausibly involves a mismatch between
the visible or intended task state and the state recorded by the environment or
automatic scoring process, including environment reset or nondeterminism, stale
sessions, unavailable artifacts, or similar environment-mediated issues.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</span></td>

<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Supplemental Analysis</h2>

<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Task-to-Economic-Value Mapping</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section expands on the task-to-economic-value mapping summarized in
Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Professional-domain distribution. ‣ 2.2.1 Task Statistics ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, describing how each task is assigned
to an occupation family and how mapping uncertainty is recorded through
confidence labels.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt an agent-assisted rule-based procedure to map each task to a SOC
major group.
After extracting the <span id="A7.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> task instructions and application metadata,
we use an LLM, GPT-5.5, to help define a set of occupation-family rules,
each linked to a SOC major group and specified through keywords,
representative applications, and O*NET-style activity descriptions.
Each task is then mapped deterministically by scoring the match between
its text and application metadata against these rules, and the
highest-scoring rule is selected as the task’s primary category.
The LLM is used only to author and refine the rule set, so the final
task-to-rule assignment is rule-based and reproducible.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Mapping uncertainty is approximated from the strength of the rule match.
Match scores are discretized into three confidence labels, namely
<em id="A7.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">high</em>, <em id="A7.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">medium</em>, and <em id="A7.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low</em>, corresponding respectively to
unambiguous matches with multiple cues, partial matches with a single
strong cue, and weak matches where no rule dominates.
Tasks in the <em id="A7.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low</em> bucket are typically generic file-management or
formatting workflows that could reasonably belong to several occupation
families.
We use these labels as qualitative uncertainty indicators during mapping audit;
they do not define a second economic-weighting scheme beyond the GDP proxy
reported in Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Professional-domain distribution. ‣ 2.2.1 Task Statistics ‣ 2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Task-Length Binning and Binary Completion Statistics</h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each <span id="A7.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">OSWorld 2.0</span> task was independently timed by two annotators
(Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Task Overview ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>).
Each annotator provided a time range (e.g., “10–30 min,” “2–5 hours”).
We convert each range to its midpoint and compute a scalar expected time per task
as the geometric mean of the two midpoints when the estimates differ, or the
common midpoint when they agree.
This yields one human-annotated expected time <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (in minutes) for each of the
108 tasks.
We sort tasks by <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and split at the 25th, 50th, 75th, and 85th percentiles,
defining five bins: <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,45)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>45</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,45)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[45,90)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>90</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[45,90)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="[90,137)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>90,137</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[90,137)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="[137,163)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>137,163</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[137,163)</annotation></semantics></math>, and
<math id="A7.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[163,360]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>163,360</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[163,360]</annotation></semantics></math> minutes (sizes: 25, 21, 24, 21, and 17 tasks).
Because annotators chose from discrete time ranges, many tasks share identical
<math id="A7.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> values; quartile boundaries alone leave too many tasks in the longest bin.
The additional 85th-percentile cut separates this tail into two smaller, more
balanced bins.
All results use the 500-step budget with each model configured at its maximum
reasoning effort.
Binary completion is defined as a fine-grained partial score
(Section <a href="#S2.SS1.SSS3" title="2.1.3 Evaluation Protocol ‣ 2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.3</span></a>) of 1.00, i.e., all scoring checkpoints are
fully satisfied.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.T21" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 21: </span>Binary completion accuracy (%) by human-annotated expected task time.</figcaption>
<table id="A7.T21.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A7.T21.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A7.T21.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"></th>
<td id="A7.T21.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" colspan="5">Human Expected Time (min)</td></tr>
<tr id="A7.T21.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A7.T21.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">Model</th>

</section>
<section id="A7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.3 </span>Challenge Exposure Attribution Details</h3>

<div id="A7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix reports the detailed exposure attribution behind
Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier models have opposite capability profiles. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.
The unit of annotation is a domain-task pair, not a task alone: because
challenge tags overlap, the same trajectory can be diagnostic for one domain
and <em id="A7.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Untested</em> for another.
The three labels are <em id="A7.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Handled</em>, <em id="A7.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Blocked</em>, and <em id="A7.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Untested</em>, as
defined in Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Binary completion rate collapses as the task horizon grows. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
We avoid repeating the aggregate counts already visualized in
Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Failures cluster on hidden-state phenomena, while the two frontier models have opposite capability profiles. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>; the full task-ID-level
attribution, including aggregate counts, is available in the generated CSV
artifact.
Here we report representative evidence that clarifies how the labels were
assigned.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.T22" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 22: </span>Representative task-level evidence for the exposure labels.
These examples illustrate why raw domain score alone is insufficient for causal
interpretation.</figcaption>

<section id="A7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.4 </span>Raw Challenge-Phenomenon Scores</h3>

<div id="A7.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A7.T23" title="Table 23 ‣ G.4 Raw Challenge-Phenomenon Scores ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a> reports raw 500-step
partial/binary scores for each phenomenon.
These scores are useful as a descriptive outcome table, but they should be read
alongside the exposure attribution in
Appendix <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Challenge Exposure Attribution Details ‣ Appendix G Supplemental Analysis ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a>: raw scores can be
confounded by failures outside the intended phenomenon or by shortcut routes that
do not provide valid evidence about the challenge mechanism.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.T23" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 23: </span>Raw 500-step model-by-phenomenon scores.
Each cell is partial score / binary success rate in percent.
Tags are non-exclusive, so the same task may appear in multiple rows.</figcaption>

<th id="A7.T23.2.1.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">Conflict</th>
<th id="A7.T23.2.1.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">39</th>

<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Case Studies</h2>

<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories</h3>

<section id="A8.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">H.1.1 </span>Task 008: Expense Reimbursement</h4>

<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This subsection traces the key steps of an agent solving the expense reimbursement
task (<span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task 008</span>) as a concrete illustration of the long-horizon,
multi-application structure discussed in
Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>.
The task instruction is:</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<blockquote id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“Please help me submit a reimbursement claim in the ExpenseFlow system.
I attended NeurIPS 2025 and also gave a talk at Stanford, and I need to get my
costs reimbursed, including conference registration, flights, and hotel.
The supporting documents should be in my MailHub inbox, and you can cross-check
the charges in my VaultBank account; I also have some additional materials saved
on my Desktop.
I’ve already opened the Oracle ExpenseFlow reimbursement guideline for you,
please follow it step by step, fill out the expense report, prepare and upload
required attachments, and submit the claim.
One more thing, you may refer to my previously submitted report for my personal
particulars.”</em></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The full trajectory runs for <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">493 steps</span> across five applications.
The annotated key steps below show both the action taken and its screenshot,
illustrating how the agent must continuously switch context and synthesize
information gathered from prior steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#A8.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ H.1.1 Task 008: Expense Reimbursement ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> and <a href="#A8.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ H.1.1 Task 008: Expense Reimbursement ‣ H.1 Representative Long-Horizon Trajectories ‣ Appendix H Case Studies ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>
show two representative input artifacts from this task that illustrate the
information-density and visual-complexity properties discussed in
Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Task Design and Construction ‣ 2 OSWorld 2.0 Benchmark ‣ OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step_airbnb_menlopark.png" id="A8.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span>A real Airbnb receipt email (Menlo Park, 4 nights).
The price breakdown lists the nightly rate ($461.50<math id="A8.F14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4 = $1,846.00),
service fee ($260.61), and taxes ($247.38) separately before the total
($2,353.99).
The agent must identify the total rather than one of the intermediate figures,
which is a source of error not present in synthetically generated receipts.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A8.F15" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step_airline_ticket.png" id="A8.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>A real airline e-ticket (United Airlines HKG–SFO) embedded in a
supplementary document template.
The multi-page layout includes branded formatting, a fare summary with itemized
charges, and baggage policy details—information density and visual structure
that model-generated documents do not replicate.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Instruction:</span> The agent receives the task above with the
Guidelines for Overseas Travel Reimbursement pre-opened in LibreOffice Writer,
and browser tabs for MailHub, VaultBank, and ExpenseFlow already loaded.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 1 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">screenshot</span> (LibreOffice Writer):</span> The agent
observes the initial state: the reimbursement policy document is open, and three
web applications (MailHub, VaultBank, ExpenseFlow) are pre-loaded in browser
tabs.
Before taking any action it must decide where to start and how to structure the
entire workflow.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F16" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step01_guideline.png" id="A8.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>Step 1 (initial state): the “Guidelines for Overseas Travel
Reimbursement” policy document in LibreOffice Writer, with MailHub, VaultBank,
and ExpenseFlow tabs pre-loaded in the browser.
The agent sees five applications and must plan the full workflow before acting.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 9 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span> (LibreOffice Writer):</span> After
scrolling through the policy, the agent reaches the Natural Account and
Step 4 Review sections.
These pages specify the exact account codes that must be entered for each
expense type (e.g., Conference – Airfare: 10120; Conference – Subsistence
Allowance: 10148) and the document upload requirements.
This information cannot be guessed and must be read before any form field can
be filled correctly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F17" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step02_natural_account.png" id="A8.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span>Step 9: the Natural Account and Review sections of the reimbursement
policy in LibreOffice Writer.
The agent reads the expense-type-to-account-code mapping and the attachment
upload instructions, both of which are required to complete the ExpenseFlow
form.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 10 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p8.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (MailHub):</span> After
internalizing the policy the agent switches to MailHub.
The inbox contains emails from NeurIPS Proceedings, Cathay Pacific (two
itineraries), Stanford, and Airbnb (two properties).
The agent must determine which emails are relevant and what information to
extract from each.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F18" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step03_mailhub_inbox.png" id="A8.F18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 18: </span>Step 10: the MailHub inbox showing receipts and e-tickets for
NeurIPS registration, Cathay Pacific flights, and Airbnb stays, all required
as evidence for the reimbursement claim.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 97 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p9.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (MailHub):</span> The agent opens
the Airbnb receipt for the San Diego stay (3 nights, $1,230.62 USD).
It must match this amount to a VaultBank transaction, classify it under the
correct subsistence-allowance policy rule, and later include it as an
attachment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F19" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step04_airbnb_receipt.png" id="A8.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 19: </span>Step 97: the Airbnb San Diego receipt email in MailHub (Receipt
ID RCKTFCWNDA, 22/11/2025, total $1,230.62 USD).
The agent reads the booking dates and amount to cross-check against VaultBank
and enter the correct per-diem values in the expense form.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 102 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p10.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (MailHub):</span> The agent opens
the Airbnb receipt for the Menlo Park stay (4 nights, $2,353.99 USD).
This email illustrates the information-density challenge of real artifacts:
the price breakdown lists a nightly rate ($461.50<math id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4), a service fee
($260.61), and taxes ($247.38) before arriving at the total, so the agent
must identify the correct value to enter rather than reading a single obvious
number.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F20" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step_airbnb_menlopark.png" id="A8.F20.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 20: </span>Step 102: the Airbnb Menlo Park receipt email (4 nights,
$2,353.99 USD total).
The price breakdown itemizes nightly rate, service fee, and taxes separately;
the agent must extract the total and cross-check it against the corresponding
VaultBank charge.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 139 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p11.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (ExpenseFlow):</span> The agent
navigates to ExpenseFlow and opens a previously submitted expense report to
retrieve the employee number (00116802), cost center (14700), and other personal
identifiers required for the new report header.
This information is not stated in the task instruction and cannot be found in
any email.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F21" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step06_expenseflow_prev.png" id="A8.F21.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 21: </span>Step 139: the ExpenseFlow Reports dashboard.
The agent opens a prior submission to extract personal identifiers (employee
number, cost center) that are not available anywhere else in the environment.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 249 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p12.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (VaultBank):</span> The agent
filters VaultBank transactions by the “Travel” category, immediately
surfacing the four relevant charges: two Cathay Pacific flights and two Airbnb
bookings.
Cross-checking these against the email receipts confirms the amounts and
satisfies the policy requirement that all charges be verified against bank
records before submission.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F22" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step05_vaultbank_travel.png" id="A8.F22.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 22: </span>Step 249: VaultBank transactions filtered by the Travel category,
showing the two Cathay Pacific flight charges and two Airbnb accommodation
charges.
The agent verifies each amount against the corresponding email receipt before
entering it in the expense form.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 274 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">type</span> (Terminal):</span> Before filling in
the expense form, the agent writes and executes a Python script using
<span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">python-docx</span> to assemble three required attachment documents
(<span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">purpose_of_travel.docx</span>, <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transportation.docx</span>,
<span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p13.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">accommodation.docx</span>), each embedding screenshots of the relevant
evidence gathered in earlier steps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F23" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step07_terminal_docs.png" id="A8.F23.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 23: </span>Step 274: the terminal after running a Python script that generates
three <span id="A8.F23.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.docx</span> attachment files embedding evidence screenshots.
These documents are uploaded to the expense report in the final submission
step.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 290 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p14.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (ExpenseFlow):</span> The agent
fills in the General Information header of a new expense report: employee name,
cost center, reimbursement currency (HKD), and the “Overseas_Travelling”
template, which controls the available expense types and the policy Notes that
must be acknowledged.
Each of these fields was derived from a different earlier step.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F24" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step08_expense_general.png" id="A8.F24.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 24: </span>Step 290: the ExpenseFlow Create Expense Report – General Information
form, with employee name, cost center, and template filled in from information
gathered across LibreOffice, MailHub, and the previous ExpenseFlow report.
The policy Notes section (20 items) is visible and must be acknowledged before
proceeding.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p15" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 492 — <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p15.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">left_click</span> (ExpenseFlow):</span> After filling
five expense lines with verified amounts and categories, setting per-line
allocations, attaching the three supporting documents, and selecting an
approver, the agent submits the report.
The submitted report number is <span id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p15.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ER-2026-0530-001</span>, and the task achieves
a partial score of 0.76.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F25" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.29537v2/figure/traj008_step09_submitted.png" id="A8.F25.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/228;" width="405" height="228" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 25: </span>Step 492: the submitted ExpenseFlow expense report
(<span id="A8.F25.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ER-2026-0530-001</span>) with five expense lines, per-line allocations,
approver assignment, and three attached documents.
The partial score of 0.76 reflects successful form submission with minor
discrepancies in per-diem location and a few missing attachment images.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.SS1.SSS1.p16" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
